title: The 2035 Women’s World Cup has huge potential for women and girls in UK
summary: Maximising the societal impact of the tournament, especially combating misogyny, should be a top priority The announcement that the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has finally come and, if we aim high enough, it could have a massive societal impact. Confirmation was a foregone conclusion – the UK was the only bidder – but that did not mean the submission was complacent or lacked ambition. Continue reading...

title: Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are | Jonathan Wilson
summary: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

title: Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances | Sean Ingle
summary: Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad “They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was ESPN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI. Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “ historique ” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? Because their younger squads might be more focused on Vice City than their opponents, and therefore play with less intensity as a result. By Monday that forecast had been liked tens of thousands of times. Continue reading...

title: Sport of kings will be going to the dogs if horse racing is complacent on welfare
summary: Latest greyhound racing blow is a wake-up call with new five-year plan keeping RSPCA on side for now Britain’s greyhound racing industry woke up on Monday to the news that the Racing Post, the daily trade newspaper that has carried extensive coverage of the sport since its launch in 1986, will drop both editorial and greyhound racecards in its print edition from 10 December. In a letter to Racing Post readers, Tom Kerr, its editor, said that it had been an “immensely difficult decision” and blamed “tax rises that have hit betting shops [which] have put pressure on the whole industry,” adding that “like other businesses, we have to make hard choices about where we focus our resources.” Five members of staff are expected to lose their jobs as a result of the decision. title: Pat Cash on the Davis Cup in the 1980s: ‘It felt like you were going to war’
summary: One of Australia’s greatest tennis players remembers being pelted with coins, tampering with nets and wanting to ‘beat these fuckers’ This year’s Davis Cup Finals begin in Bologna on Tuesday but the culmination of the oldest team competition in tennis will probably pass most Australian sports fans by. Few countries can challenge Australia’s history in the Davis Cup; they reached the final every year between 1938 and 1968 and have won the event 28 times, second only to the United States.
